paras: The attempted lynching of Thomas Hourigan was an armed mob's attack on the jail at Lebanon, Kentucky, on the night of Tuesday, June 26, 1888, aimed at hanging a physician held for killing his brother-in-law. The mob battered down his cell door but scattered when an officer fired a pistol into it, and Hourigan escaped unhurt. Kentucky papers and a Louisville wire dispatch treated it as a narrow escape, which one headline called "A Close Call From a Mob."

Hourigan, a physician at Riley, a small town in Marion County about nine miles east of Lebanon, shot and killed his brother-in-law Samuel Hays, 21, on Saturday evening, April 28, 1888. According to the dispatches, the two quarreled over a small debt Hourigan owed, put by the Stanford Interior Journal at $2.50, and Hays belonged to one of the wealthiest families in the county. Hourigan surrendered at Lebanon and, according to an Indianapolis report, claimed self-defense.

Within days he was "spirited off" to the Louisville jail to keep a mob from reaching him, and he was to be returned to Lebanon for his examining trial. By the end of June a murder indictment had been found against him, and the Hickman Courier wrote that public opinion had run high against him and that mob violence had been talked of since the killing.

The fullest account, printed in the Hickman Courier, says that soon after ten o'clock Hourigan's 70-year-old father, who lived on the turnpike about ten miles from Lebanon, learned that an organized party was marching on the jail and rode into town to warn the jailer. Marshal Torrel was in charge when he arrived, and the prisoner was roused and dressed, but it was too late to get him away, and he was locked back in his cell.

The Courier put the mob at forty masked men, one carrying a rope and the rest heavily armed, while the Interior Journal reported 30 armed men. When the jailer refused to give up the keys, the leaders brought a battering ram and broke down the iron door of Hourigan's cell as he screamed for help. At that moment, in the Courier's account, Deputy Sheriff Faulkner fired his pistol point blank into the attackers, who scattered; the Louisville wire credited "a volley from the sheriff's revolver." The town bell was rung and citizens came to the jailer's aid, and the mob vanished.

No report of arrests or of any inquiry into the mob appears in the coverage. By late November Hourigan was again being held in the Louisville jail "to keep him from being mobbed," and he was brought back to Lebanon for trial under a strong guard. He then obtained a change of venue from Marion to Taylor County and was returned to Louisville; no report of the trial's outcome was found.

The attack reached readers mainly through a Louisville dispatch dated June 28, which the Maysville Evening Bulletin headed "A Close Call From a Mob" and the Waterbury Evening Democrat in Connecticut ran in shorter form as "They Tried to Lynch Him." The wire stressed the drama of the rescue, saying the prisoner was saved "at the last moment" and was "badly frightened."

The Stanford Interior Journal, which had earlier called Hourigan "the fellow who murdered his brother-in-law," reported that the mob was "successfully resisted" and added that the killing had happened "under circumstances that did not warrant so desperate a course." A week later the Hickman Courier gave the longest version in its Kentucky news column, describing the mob as "well organized and drilled" and seemingly "composed of a better class of men." When the killing was first reported, the Maysville Evening Bulletin had joked that jailing Hourigan was "an unjustifiable interference with man's private business."

Accounts differ on the size of the mob, 30 armed men in the Interior Journal and forty masked men in the Hickman Courier, and on who fired, the sheriff in the wire and Deputy Sheriff Faulkner in the Courier, whose fuller account names the officer.

reader.title: Attempted lynching of Thomas Hourigan
bases: An armed, masked mob broke into the Lebanon jail and battered down a cell door to take and hang a prisoner charged with murder, and was driven off by an officer's pistol fire (A7, A9, A10).

A mob of 30 to 40 men tried to take Hourigan from jail and hang him for the killing of his brother-in-law, which meets every part of the definition except a death: he was not harmed (A7, A9, A10). It was an attempted lynching.

A Louisville wire (A7, A8), a Stanford, Ky., weekly brief (A9) and a separate, much longer Kentucky account (A10) agree on a mob attack on the Lebanon jail that was repelled by an officer's gunfire; they differ only on mob size and which officer fired.

accounts.label: Louisville wire
accounts.gist: A mob at Lebanon battered down the cell doors in a determined effort to lynch Hourigan; a volley from the sheriff's revolver scattered the crowd until law-abiding citizens came to the rescue.

accounts.label: Stanford Interior Journal brief
accounts.gist: Thirty armed men tried to take Hourigan from jail and hang him but were successfully resisted; the paper added that the killing had been unwarranted.

accounts.label: Hickman Courier state news
accounts.gist: Forty masked men, organized and drilled, demanded Hourigan after his father warned the jail; the jailer refused the keys, the mob rammed the cell door down, and Deputy Sheriff Faulkner fired into them; the town bell brought citizens to the jailer's aid.

framing.detail: The Louisville wire ran as 'A Close Call From a Mob' in Maysville and 'They Tried to Lynch Him' in Waterbury, Conn., stressing the narrow escape and the sheriff's volley.
The Interior Journal reported the mob was 'successfully resisted' but called Hourigan 'the fellow who murdered his brother-in-law' and said the killing was unwarranted.
The Hickman Courier told the story in detail, calling the mob well organized, 'a better class of men', and saying public opinion had 'run high against tho [the] murderer'.

conflicts.note: Both are Kentucky papers at second hand; neither is a Lebanon report.

versions.value: the sheriff fired a volley from his revolver
Deputy Sheriff Faulkner fired his pistol into the mob

conflicts.note: The Hickman Courier account is fuller and names the officer; the wire may have used 'sheriff' loosely.
Spelling varies; Hays is the most common form.
